The shipment's actual weight is exactly 50.0 kg, which already meets and exceeds the 25 kg chargeable-weight floor (§1), so chargeable weight is 50.0 kg. Clause §2 sets a per-kg rate for consignments "under 50 kg" (strict less-than) and a separate rate for consignments "over 50 kg" (strict greater-than). A consignment at exactly 50 kg satisfies neither condition as literally written, so the contract does not state a per-kg rate applicable to this consignment. This is not a case where the shipment facts are unclear -- the facts are certain -- but the rate-band boundaries in §2 leave a genuine textual gap at exactly 50 kg, which the rate card's own recorded ambiguities list confirms (it flags this exact scenario). Because two readings are plausible (rounding down to the "under 50kg" band, or up to the "over 50kg" band) and neither is compelled by the text, I cannot determine which rate governs, so no expected amount can be soundly derived. This matches the policy default for ambiguous_line findings: escalate rather than pick a band that isn't actually written in the contract.

The pricing trace correctly applies the contract to this shipment: 260 kg billed weight falls unambiguously within the 'up to and including 500 kg' band (§1) at ₹18/km over the 800 km lane, the express service premium of 15% applies per §2 (service_level is express), and the 12% fuel surcharge compounds on base freight plus the express premium per §3. No accessorial (§4) fired since special_handling is empty, and §5 bars any charge outside the schedule. This chain reproduces the expected amount exactly, leaving the billed amount unsupported by any contract mechanism. Unlike the fractional-weight ambiguity noted elsewhere in the rate card, 260 kg is squarely inside the lower band with no boundary issue, so there is no genuine interpretive gap here — the overcharge is a clean, determinable billing error.

Recomputing the freight charge from the shipment facts and contract text confirms the pricing trace: 700 kg falls in the "501 kg to 2,000 kg" band (§1), so base freight is ₹24/km × 800 km = 19,200. Express premium (§2) correctly does not fire since service_level is "standard," not "express." Fuel surcharge (§3) correctly applies 12% to the 19,200 base freight, adding 2,304, for a freight charge of 21,504. No accessorial applies — special_handling is empty, so residential delivery (§4) is correctly not triggered — and §5 is explicit that no other accessorial charges are payable under this agreement absent a prior written rate confirmation, none of which is evidenced here. The billed amount exceeds this fully-supported, contract-traced total, and nothing in the contract or shipment record accounts for the difference. This is a determinable overcharge, not an ambiguous case: every band, premium, and surcharge in the trace checks out against the verbatim contract text, so the excess is simply unsupported billing.

Consignment FF-8003, matched to a single shipment (SH-4003), appears identically on two separate Falcon invoices (FALCON-2026-07A block 3 and FALCON-2026-07B block 8), each billed at the same amount with pricing independently determined and matching the contract's expected freight for this consignment. The shipment record shows one ship date, one delivery event (delivered 2026-07-06), and no indication of a re-delivery, correction, or split shipment that would justify two separate freight charges under §1 (base freight is charged per kilometre of the booked lane distance for the consignment). Clause 5's whitelist further confirms nothing beyond the scheduled freight/accessorial items in §§1-4 is payable absent a written rate confirmation, and no such confirmation or explanation for a second charge appears in the evidence. With no shipment or invoice evidence explaining a legitimate basis for billing the same consignment's freight twice, the second occurrence is an unauthorized duplicate charge.

invoice_findings.description: invoice qualifies for 'Volume incentive discount' under every computable date basis (40 consignments, threshold gt 12), but the carrier's declared discount is 0.0
invoice_findings.justification: Under §5, the 5% volume incentive discount applies to any calendar month in which BlueFin tendered more than 12 consignments. All three candidate counting bases (by invoice document, by booking-date calendar month, and by ship-date calendar month) independently agree this invoice covers 40 consignments, well above the >12 threshold, so entitlement to the discount is not in question. However, the carrier declared a discount of 0.0, which appears to be an oversight or omission on their part. The exact rupee shortfall cannot yet be computed because one line on this invoice remains pricing-undetermined; the 5% discount is applied to the invoice total per §5, and that total is not yet finalized. This is not a case a colleague can act on with a concrete figure today, so it must be escalated rather than disputed until the blocking line is resolved and the invoice total (and thus the discount shortfall) can be computed.
